lead: An open control volume has streams crossing its boundary. Each stream carries entropy at the rate ṁs, heat carries entropy at the rate Q/T, and friction, mixing and finite temperature gaps inside create more. The entropy balance adds these terms. At steady state nothing accumulates, so the generation equals entropy out minus entropy in. Engineers use it to test turbines, compressors, nozzles and heat exchangers.
prereq: You need: entropy and the Clausius inequality and the steady-flow mass and energy balances from the first-law chapters.

blocks.text: Take a control volume (CV), a fixed region in space. Let m<sub>i</sub> be mass flow at inlet i in kg/s and s<sub>i</sub> its specific entropy in kJ/(kg·K). Let m<sub>e</sub> and s<sub>e</sub> be the same at outlet e. Let Q<sub>j</sub> be heat rate into the CV across boundary j in kW, and T<sub>j</sub> the absolute temperature of that boundary in K. Let S<sub>CV</sub> be total entropy inside the CV in kJ/K, and S<sub>gen</sub> the entropy generation rate in kW/K. The balance is:
dS<sub>CV</sub>/dt = Σ m<sub>i</sub> s<sub>i</sub> − Σ m<sub>e</sub> s<sub>e</sub> + Σ Q<sub>j</sub>/T<sub>j</sub> + S<sub>gen</sub>
blocks.where: S<sub>CV</sub> is total entropy inside the CV in kJ/K; t is time in s; m<sub>i</sub> is inlet mass flow in kg/s; s<sub>i</sub> is inlet specific entropy in kJ/(kg·K); m<sub>e</sub> and s<sub>e</sub> are outlet mass flow and specific entropy; Q<sub>j</sub> is heat rate into the CV in kW; T<sub>j</sub> is the uniform absolute temperature of boundary j in K; if the boundary temperature varies, replace Q<sub>j</sub>/T<sub>j</sub> by the integral ∫ δQ/T over that boundary; S<sub>gen</sub> is entropy generation rate in kW/K.

blocks.text: The first term is accumulation. The next two are entropy carried by flow. The heat term is entropy carried by heat; use T<sub>j</sub> in kelvin. S<sub>gen</sub> comes from irreversibility inside: friction, mixing, chemical reaction, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference. The second law gives S<sub>gen</sub> ≥ 0, with equality only for a reversible process. S<sub>gen</sub> is not a state property; it is fixed by the process. At steady state dS<sub>CV</sub>/dt = 0, so S<sub>gen</sub> = Σ m<sub>e</sub> s<sub>e</sub> − Σ m<sub>i</sub> s<sub>i</sub> − Σ Q<sub>j</sub>/T<sub>j</sub>. A negative computed S<sub>gen</sub> means the data or sign convention is wrong.
For one inlet and one outlet, steady, adiabatic (Q<sub>j</sub> = 0), the balance reduces to:

blocks.where: m is mass flow in kg/s; s<sub>in</sub> and s<sub>out</sub> are inlet and outlet specific entropies in kJ/(kg·K); S<sub>gen</sub> is entropy generation rate in kW/K.

blocks.text: Work and kinetic energy do not appear: entropy crosses only with mass and heat. A real adiabatic turbine has s<sub>out</sub> > s<sub>in</sub> because friction and losses generate entropy; the ideal isentropic turbine sets s<sub>out</sub> = s<sub>in</sub> and S<sub>gen</sub> = 0. A compressor needs work; if adiabatic, the same formula applies and real s<sub>out</sub> > s<sub>in</sub>. If the compressor is cooled, heat leaves, so Q<sub>j</sub> is negative; use the full balance. A nozzle has no work and is often adiabatic: S<sub>gen</sub> = m(s<sub>out</sub> − s<sub>in</sub>), and an ideal nozzle is isentropic.

For a two-stream heat exchanger with no external heat, enclose both streams in the CV. Then S<sub>gen</sub> = m<sub>h</sub>(s<sub>h,out</sub> − s<sub>h,in</sub>) + m<sub>c</sub>(s<sub>c,out</sub> − s<sub>c,in</sub>). Internal heat from hot to cold stays inside the CV and does not appear as Q<sub>j</sub>. If the exchanger also loses heat to the room, the leak raises the generation: S<sub>gen</sub> = m<sub>h</sub>(s<sub>h,out</sub> − s<sub>h,in</sub>) + m<sub>c</sub>(s<sub>c,out</sub> − s<sub>c,in</sub>) − Q<sub>room</sub>/T<sub>room</sub>, with Q<sub>room</sub> negative when heat leaves, so the last term is positive. Some syllabi call the steady balance the second law for a control volume.

items: Draw the CV and mark every inlet, outlet and heat crossing.
Write m and s for each stream, using kJ/(kg·K).
Write each Q<sub>j</sub> as positive into the CV and T<sub>j</sub> in K.
Put terms in the balance and solve for S<sub>gen</sub>. Check units and sign.

blocks.text: Check units: kg/s × kJ/(kg·K) = kW/K; kW divided by K = kW/K. Check sign: Sgen cannot be negative. For a reversible adiabatic device, Sgen = 0. For a real adiabatic device, outlet specific entropy is greater than inlet. The same Sgen becomes lost work when multiplied by T₀; see lost work and ideal work.

spec.aria: A turbine inside a dashed control volume: steam enters at 3 MPa and 400 degrees with 13.847 kW/K of entropy, leaves at 50 kPa with 14.536 kW/K, gives 1403 kW of power, and generates 0.689 kW/K.

examples.question: Steam at 2 kg/s enters an adiabatic turbine at 3 MPa and 400 °C (s<sub>in</sub> = 6.9233 kJ/(kg·K), h<sub>in</sub> = 3231.6 kJ/kg) and leaves at 50 kPa with quality 0.95 (at 50 kPa: s<sub>f</sub> = 1.0910, s<sub>g</sub> = 7.5930 kJ/(kg·K), h<sub>f</sub> = 340.5, h<sub>g</sub> = 2645.2 kJ/kg). Find the entropy generation rate and the power, and say whether the turbine is reversible.
steps: Choose a CV around the turbine. Steady flow: dS<sub>CV</sub>/dt = 0. One inlet, one outlet, adiabatic: Q<sub>j</sub> = 0, so 0 = m s<sub>in</sub> − m s<sub>out</sub> + S<sub>gen</sub>.
Exit entropy: s<sub>out</sub> = s<sub>f</sub> + x(s<sub>g</sub> − s<sub>f</sub>) = 1.0910 + 0.95 × 6.5020 = 7.2679 kJ/(kg·K).
Exit enthalpy: h<sub>out</sub> = h<sub>f</sub> + x(h<sub>g</sub> − h<sub>f</sub>) = 340.5 + 0.95 × 2304.7 = 2530.0 kJ/kg. Power = m(h<sub>in</sub> − h<sub>out</sub>) = 2 × 701.6 = 1403 kW.
For comparison, an isentropic exit at 50 kPa has x = (6.9233 − 1.0910)/6.5020 = 0.897 and h = 2407.8 kJ/kg, so the turbine efficiency is 701.6/823.8 = 0.85.
examples.answer: S<sub>gen</sub> = 0.689 kW/K and the turbine gives 1403 kW. S<sub>gen</sub> > 0, so it is irreversible; its isentropic efficiency is about 85 %.

examples.question: In an insulated counter-flow heat exchanger, 1 kg/s of hot water cools from 90 °C to 50 °C and heats 2 kg/s of cold water that enters at 20 °C. Take c = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K) for both streams. Find the cold-water outlet temperature and S<sub>gen</sub>.
steps: Energy balance: 1 × 4.18 × (90 − 50) = 2 × 4.18 × (T − 20), so T − 20 = 20 and the cold stream leaves at 40 °C.
Liquid entropy change: Δs = c ln(T₂/T₁) with T in kelvin.
No heat crosses the outer boundary, so S<sub>gen</sub> = −0.4878 + 0.5517 = 0.0639 kW/K. Heat flowing down a 30 K gap made this entropy.
examples.answer: The cold water leaves at 40 °C and S<sub>gen</sub> = 0.064 kW/K.

traps: Forgetting S<sub>gen</sub> and treating an adiabatic real turbine as isentropic. A real adiabatic turbine has s<sub>out</sub> > s<sub>in</sub>.
Reversing the order: for an adiabatic device, S<sub>gen</sub> = m(s<sub>out</sub> − s<sub>in</sub>), not m(s<sub>in</sub> − s<sub>out</sub>). A negative answer is impossible.
Using the fluid temperature instead of the boundary temperature in Q<sub>j</sub>/T<sub>j</sub>. The temperature is the absolute temperature where heat crosses the CV boundary, in K.
Mixing up mass flow and total mass. ṁs has units kg/s × kJ/(kg·K) = kW/K; using kg instead of kg/s gives kJ/K, a total, not a rate.
Setting S<sub>gen</sub> = 0 for a two-stream heat exchanger because there is no external heat. Internal heat exchange can still generate entropy; add the entropy changes of both streams.

quiz.q: Define entropy generation rate S<sub>gen</sub> and state its sign rule.
quiz.a: S<sub>gen</sub> is the rate of entropy created inside a control volume by irreversibility, in kW/K. The second law requires S<sub>gen</sub> ≥ 0, with equality only for a reversible process.

quiz.q: Why must s<sub>out</sub> be greater than s<sub>in</sub> for a real adiabatic turbine with one inlet and one outlet?
quiz.a: For steady adiabatic flow, S<sub>gen</sub> = m(s<sub>out</sub> − s<sub>in</sub>). Since m > 0 and S<sub>gen</sub> ≥ 0, s<sub>out</sub> ≥ s<sub>in</sub>. Friction and losses make the real turbine irreversible, so s<sub>out</sub> > s<sub>in</sub>.

quiz.q: Steam flows at 1.5 kg/s through an adiabatic nozzle. Inlet specific entropy is 6.8 kJ/(kg·K); outlet specific entropy is 7.1 kJ/(kg·K). Find S<sub>gen</sub>.

An adiabatic two-stream heat exchanger has hot stream 1 kg/s with s<sub>h,in</sub> = 2.0 and s<sub>h,out</sub> = 1.6 kJ/(kg·K), and cold stream 1 kg/s with s<sub>c,in</sub> = 0.8 and s<sub>c,out</sub> = 1.3 kJ/(kg·K). Find S<sub>gen</sub> and say whether the data are possible.
quiz.a: S<sub>gen</sub> = 1(1.6 − 2.0) + 1(1.3 − 0.8) = −0.4 + 0.5 = 0.1 kW/K. It is positive, so the data are possible.

quiz.q: A compressor has m = 0.5 kg/s, s<sub>in</sub> = 1.8 and s<sub>out</sub> = 2.0 kJ/(kg·K). It loses 10 kW of heat at a boundary at 300 K. Find S<sub>gen</sub>.
quiz.a: Heat into CV is Q = −10 kW. S<sub>gen</sub> = m(s<sub>out</sub> − s<sub>in</sub>) − Q/T = 0.5(2.0 − 1.8) − (−10)/300 = 0.1 + 0.0333 = 0.1333 kW/K.

quiz.q: A claim says an adiabatic nozzle has s<sub>out</sub> < s<sub>in</sub>. Is this possible? Explain with the entropy balance.
quiz.a: No. For steady adiabatic one-inlet one-outlet flow, S<sub>gen</sub> = m(s<sub>out</sub> − s<sub>in</sub>). If s<sub>out</sub> < s<sub>in</sub>, then S<sub>gen</sub> < 0, which violates the second law. Therefore s<sub>out</sub> ≥ s<sub>in</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plant audits compute entropy generation stream by stream to rank the losses in a steam network, and CFD codes map local entropy generation to improve ducts and compact exchangers. Search for "entropy generation minimisation".
